title: Validity, Implication and the Two-Element Countermodel
quickIdea: A implies B in first-order logic when every interpretation that makes A true makes B true. One small countermodel kills an option, so domains of size two decide most GATE questions.
remember: A implies B is valid exactly when A and not B is unsatisfiable, and exactly when the formula A implies B is valid.

Valid schemas: (for all x P(x)) implies there exists x P(x) over a non-empty domain; (there exists y for all x R(x, y)) implies (for all x there exists y R(x, y)); for all x (P(x) implies Q(x)) implies ((for all x P(x)) implies (for all x Q(x))); there exists x (P(x) and Q(x)) implies (there exists x P(x) and there exists x Q(x)).

Invalid schemas: ((for all x P(x)) implies (for all x Q(x))) does not imply for all x (P(x) implies Q(x)); for all x (P(x) or Q(x)) does not imply (for all x P(x) or for all x Q(x)); (there exists x P(x) and there exists x Q(x)) does not imply there exists x (P(x) and Q(x)); for all x there exists y R(x, y) does not imply there exists y for all x R(x, y).
The universal distributes over and, the existential over or; the other two combinations fail.
To refute an option, build one interpretation: choose a small domain, then assign the predicates so the premise is true and the conclusion false.
A disjunction is false only when both parts are false; that single fact drives the falsification method.

example.prompt: Show that for all x (p(x) or q(x)) does not imply (for all x p(x) or for all x q(x)).
example.work: Domain {1, 2}. Make p true only at 1 and q true only at 2. Then every element satisfies p or q, so the premise is true; but p fails at 2 and q fails at 1, so neither universal on the right holds.
example.answer: The premise is true and the conclusion false, so the implication is invalid.

gateAngle: GATE CS 2003 Q.32 asks which formula is valid (answer D), GATE CS 2016 Set 2 Q.27 asks which is NOT valid (answer D, refuted by even and odd numbers), and GATE CS 2023 Q.16 asks which options imply a conjecture (B and C). All three are settled by two-element or integer countermodels.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: See the three linked PYQs: GATE 2003 Q.32, GATE 2016 Set 2 Q.27 and GATE 2023 Q.16.
variations.why: Each distractor is a swapped distribution or a swapped quantifier order, which a single small model refutes.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Does (there exists x p(x) and there exists x q(x)) imply there exists x (p(x) and q(x))?
variations.why: Domain {1, 2} with p true only at 1 and q true only at 2 makes the premise true and the conclusion false: the two witnesses can be different elements.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Is (there exists y for all x R(x, y)) implies (for all x there exists y R(x, y)) valid?
variations.why: If one y is related to every x, then for each x that same y is a witness for the existential, so the conclusion holds in every interpretation.

trap.what: Reading for all x (p(x) or q(x)) as (for all x p(x)) or (for all x q(x)).
trap.why: The premise lets each element choose a different disjunct; the conclusion forces one disjunct to hold for all elements.
trap.counterexample: Domain {1, 2}, p true only at 1, q true only at 2: the premise is true, the conclusion false.

check.question: Does for all x (P(x) implies Q(x)) imply ((for all x P(x)) implies (for all x Q(x)))?
check.explanation: If P implies Q pointwise and P holds everywhere, then Q holds everywhere. The converse fails, which is what GATE 2003 Q.32 option (A) tests.
